result: {"decisions":[{"point":"D2","problem":"How to evaluate whether a detection defense is robust given varying attacker knowledge.","did":"They evaluated each defense under three threat models (zero-knowledge, perfect-knowledge, limited-knowledge) using a strong attack, an adaptive white-box attack, and a transfer-based black-box attack.","alternatives_named":["evaluating only with weak attacks like fast gradient sign and JSMA","evaluating only against an oblivious attacker"],"stated_reason":"The zero-knowledge test is the weakest threat model so failing it implies failing the others; the black-box test is only interesting if zero-knowledge failed and white-box succeeded.","quote":"In this step we generate adversarial examples with C&W’s attack and check whether the defense can detect this strong attack. This evaluation approach has the weakest threat model (the attacker is not even aware the defense is in place), so any defense should trivially be able to detect this attack."},{"point":"D2","problem":"Which attack to use for generating adversarial examples when testing the defenses.","did":"They used the C&W L2 targeted attack rather than FGS or JSMA used in the original defense papers.","alternatives_named":["Fast Gradient Sign","JSMA"],"stated_reason":"These attacks are weaker than C&W's attack, and weak attacks give a biased view of defense robustness.","quote":"Aside from C&W’s attack, the Fast Gradient Sign attack (Goodfellow et al., 2014) and JSMA (Papernot et al., 2016b) are two attacks used by some defenses for evaluation. These attacks are weaker than C&W’s attack and we do not use them for evaluation"},{"point":"D5","problem":"How to interpret the large detectable difference between natural and adversarial examples in PCA on MNIST.","did":"They investigated the cause of the difference and found it was an artifact of MNIST border pixels, not an intrinsic property of adversarial examples, and checked CIFAR.","alternatives_named":["concluding PCA is a powerful and effective detector"],"stated_reason":"Large abnormalities in data require understanding their cause; the difference arises because border pixels are nearly always zero in natural MNIST images.","quote":"At first glance, this might lead us to believe that PCA is a powerful and effective method for detecting adversarial examples. However, whenever there are large abnormalities in the data, one must be careful to understand their cause."},{"point":"D2","problem":"Whether the failure of Bhagoji's dimensionality reduction defense to improve robustness is due to the network architecture rather than the defense.","did":"They tested a second Bhagoji algorithm combining PCA projection with a convolutional network, holding architecture fixed so only dimensionality reduction varies.","alternatives_named":["comparing only the fully-connected PCA model to a convolutional baseline"],"stated_reason":"To show the result is not an artifact of fully-connected networks being less robust than convolutional ones.","quote":"This allows us to perform an experiment where the network architecture is held fixed, and the only change is whether dimensionality reduction is used or not."},{"point":"D4","problem":"What to do when the generic combined-function attack on the dropout randomization defense failed.","did":"They diagnosed that the function U is computed on probabilities F not logits Z, abandoned the single combined function, and instead changed the loss to sum over several sampled deterministic networks.","alternatives_named":["constructing a single function G to optimize over"],"stated_reason":"Because U is computed from F rather than Z, there is no good constant c, so gradient descent performs poorly.","quote":"Therefore, for this defense, we abandon the approach of constructing a single function to optimize over and instead change the loss function $\\ell$ used by the attack."},{"point":"D3","problem":"Whether a failed first attack attempt shows a defense is robust.","did":"They treated the initial 60% detection as an attack-design failure and investigated why, rather than accepting the defense as effective.","alternatives_named":["accepting that the defense detects adversarial examples"],"stated_reason":"The choice of loss function is critical; the obvious loss often makes a defense appear more robust than it is.","quote":"We discover that the specific loss function chosen is critical to effectively defeating the defense: choosing the immediately obvious loss function often results in the defense appearing significantly more robust than it actually is."},{"point":"D6","problem":"How to characterize the dropout defense's limited-knowledge result, where the transfer attack needs only 15% more distortion.","did":"They framed the result as a success of the defense under the white-box model and called it the only defense not completely broken.","alternatives_named":["calling it a failure of the defense under the black-box threat model"],"stated_reason":"It made adaptive white-box attacks nearly as hard as black-box attacks.","quote":"While this $15\\%$ increase may seem like a failure of this defense under the black-box threat model, we see this instead as a success of defense under the white-box threat model."},{"point":"D1","problem":"Which datasets to use for evaluating the defenses.","did":"They evaluated on both MNIST and CIFAR-10 and found that MNIST results do not carry over to CIFAR.","alternatives_named":["evaluating solely on MNIST"],"stated_reason":"Defenses evaluated only on MNIST were typically useless or weaker on CIFAR, so MNIST alone is not sufficient.","quote":"Future schemes need to be evaluated on multiple data sets — evaluating their security solely on MNIST is not sufficient."},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to make the limited-knowledge evaluation of Grosse's defense a fair test of transfer.","did":"They split the training set in half, giving the attacker one half with white-box access to model R1 and testing transfer to the defender's model R2 trained on the other half.","alternatives_named":["training one model on the complete training set"],"stated_reason":"The attacker should not have the exact model parameters or training data of the secured model.","quote":"Instead of training one model on the complete training set, we split the training set in half. We assume the first half is known to the attacker and the second half is used by the defender to train their network."}]}
